1.pericope_label: Not unto us, O Lord, but unto thy name give glory: but our God is in the heavens

schools.summary: Augustine grounds the refusal of glory in grace given not for preceding works but of the mercy that justifies the ungodly, and insists that the heaven meant is above all heavenly and earthly bodies, God needing no place to rest in and fearing no fall if heaven were withdrawn.

Calvin says only that the psalm was penned when the Church was deeply afflicted, and his block carries a later paragraph stacking the rival guesses at its author and occasion; Gill refers the glory entirely to God in every temporal and spiritual benefit, and applies the reproach of the heathen to the Papists of his own day.

Spurgeon fixes the psalm at the Passover and reads it as a plea that God display his power again as at the Red Sea, arguing that he will not work miracles at the demand of boasters any more than his Son came down from the cross; Henry finds boasting for ever excluded and every crown cast at the throne.

Clarke lists the manuscripts and versions that join this psalm to the preceding one, leaves author and occasion unknown, calls it a triumphal song ascribing the victory entirely to God, and reads the third verse as a confession that there was cause enough for their being abandoned to their enemies.

Ellicott traces mercy and truth to the covenant and reconstructs how real the idolater’s apparent triumph felt to a worshipper of the invisible God; Keil and Delitzsch reject the joining of the two psalms as an arrangement that condemns itself, guess an expedition against heathen enemies, and relay a conjecture that the sacrifice proceeded while the psalm was sung.

debates: Is this a psalm of its own or the end of the previous one? Clarke counts eighteen manuscripts of one collator and fifty-three of another, several ancient versions and an old Psalter that read the two together; Keil and Delitzsch report the same evidence and call the arrangement arbitrary and self-condemning, noting that a Jewish commentator favoured it and that it entered many Hebrew manuscripts; the paragraph attached to Calvin holds the continuation not improbable, since the earlier psalm ended abruptly.

What occasion produced it? Clarke calls it a triumphal song but leaves the occasion unknown; Keil and Delitzsch suppose an expedition against heathen enemies; Spurgeon fixes on its use at the Passover and its relation to the deliverance from Egypt; Calvin says only that the Church was deeply afflicted, while the paragraph attached to his block canvasses the Red Sea, the beginning of David’s reign, the story of Esther, the fiery furnace, the reign of Hezekiah and the Babylonish captivity.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch relay a conjecture they find pleasing, that the sacrifice was being offered while the psalm was sung and that partway through it a priest’s voice proclaims the gracious acceptance of that sacrifice, though they hold the change of voices begins earlier than the verse proposed.
Gill identifies the heathen who ask where their God is with the Papists of his own day.

Spurgeon observes that when Israel marched into Canaan a terror was upon all the people round about, and that the nations had shaken this dread off because there had lately been no remarkable display of miraculous power.
themes: glory refused for the self and referred to the name
a psalm whose boundaries the manuscripts dispute
an author and occasion guessed half a dozen ways
the taunt of the visible god against the invisible
heaven asserted as freedom rather than as place

4.pericope_label: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands: they that make them are like unto them

schools.summary: Gill answers the catalogue member by member against the God who hears and gives, notes that one image of a god was deliberately made without ears since it was unbecoming for the lord of all to listen to any, reports a Jewish reading of the last verse as a petition rather than a statement, and applies the whole description to the images of the Papists of his own day.

Clarke observes that the more serious heathens ridiculed idolatry themselves and quotes a satirist demanding whether the god hears and why he does not move his lips, concluding that there is no difference between the god’s statue and that of a musician whose image a tyrant had set up in a temple.

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew of the last clause denies not merely articulate speech but any utterance, and closes with a couplet distinguishing the man who moulds a sacred face from the man who asks its grace; Keil and Delitzsch call the idols dead images devoid even of the sensuous life whose organs are carved upon them, and weigh whether the words for their hands and feet are prominent subjects or absolute cases.

debates: Is the last verse a statement or a curse? Gill takes it first as describing the makers as senseless as their material, but reports that two Jewish commentators and the ancient versions alike read it as a petition, let them that make them be like unto them, which turns the description into an imprecation.
outliers: Clarke quotes a Roman satirist asking whether the god hears, and why he does not move his lips when he ought to speak, whether he is of marble or of bronze, and concluding that there is no difference between the god’s statue and that of a musician; the irony is keener, Clarke notes, because that musician was a player whose image had been erected in a temple by a tyrant’s order.
Gill reports that the image of a god in Crete was made without ears, on the ground that it was unbecoming for one who was prince and lord of all to give ear to any.
Ellicott closes the section with a couplet holding that whoever moulds a sacred face in gold or stone does not thereby make the god, but the man who asks its grace does.
themes: a catalogue of organs that do not work
idolatry ridiculed by the heathen themselves
an idol built deliberately without ears
worship as the act that makes the god
description turning into imprecation

9.pericope_label: O Israel, trust thou in the Lord: he will bless them that fear the Lord, both small and great

schools.summary: Spurgeon explains the change of person as a soliloquy, the psalmist whispering to himself the ground of his own exhortation, and tells the priests that those nearest God should trust him most; Henry identifies the third group as proselytes not of the seed of Israel, makes fear and cheerful faith companions, and notes that the priests are most struck at by enemies and so most cared for.

Gill takes the third group as proselytes of every nation on the authority of two Jewish commentators, argues that faith and fear are consistent and instances a man famous for fearing God who trusted him, and extends the priestly office to all saints under the Gospel, whose sacrifices cannot please God without faith.

Clarke reads the third group as all real penitents and sincere believers rather than as a nation or a class, takes the house of Aaron as the different orders of the priesthood, and supplies a literal rendering of the blessing verses while pointing out how many of their words are redoubled for effect; Wesley makes the third group Gentile proselytes as well as Israelites.

Ellicott glosses those that fear the Lord as all Israel, finds consummate art in the sudden change of address, and reconstructs a liturgical performance in which a priest or half the choir charges the congregation and the full choir answers with the refrain until both join in the first person; Keil and Delitzsch mark where the voice of consolation begins and becomes a voice of hope.

debates: Who are those that fear the Lord, named third after Israel and the house of Aaron? Gill denies the phrase sorts true saints from hypocrites within the first two groups and makes it proselytes of every people and nation, citing two Jewish commentators; Wesley and Henry agree that Gentile proselytes are meant; Clarke drops the ethnic question and reads all real penitents and sincere believers; Ellicott glosses the same phrase as all Israel.

Why does the psalm change person here? Ellicott finds a liturgical cause, a change in the music with a priest or one half of the choir charging the congregation and the full choir answering with the refrain, congregation and choir joining afterwards in the first person; Spurgeon finds a psychological one, the psalmist whispering to himself in a soliloquy after his own exhortation.
outliers: Ellicott compares the sudden turn to the people with the pointed application of a general truth in a sermon, and imagines the choir turning to them with a loud burst of song.
Gill argues that faith and fear are not rivals but companions, and instances a man famous for fearing God who nonetheless trusted him.
Spurgeon remarks that it is good to exhort those to faith who already have faith.
themes: a congregation addressed in three ranks
the God-fearers taken as proselytes or as the nation itself
a change of person read as liturgy or as soliloquy
ministers required to lead in confidence
reverence and reliance held to be inseparable

14.pericope_label: The heaven, even the heavens, are the Lord’s: but we will bless the Lord for evermore

schools.summary: Spurgeon gives the grant of the earth two senses without choosing, one in which God restrains his own power because he gave his creatures free agency, another in which the clause grounds the promised increase since he means his people to fill the earth; he keeps the line about the dead strictly to this world, where the tomb sends forth no voice and the choir loses its singers one by one, and closes by refusing affliction, age and death as reasons to stop praising.

Gill narrows the line about the dead at both ends, excluding the dead in sin and also the departed saints, whose souls praise God continually with the angels and are barred only from praising him with bodily organs until the resurrection, and notes that the ancient versions read the last verse as we who are alive.

Clarke dates the grant of the earth from the expulsion from paradise, restricts the dead who do not praise to the idolaters of the earlier verses, defuses the old English renderings that put hell in the last section by tracing the word to a root meaning to cover or conceal, and closes with the living standing in the place of silent fathers; Wesley reads the division of heaven and earth as a claim of title and the place of silence as the grave.

Ellicott renders the promise of increase as a heaping of blessings on them and their children and identifies the land of silence as the under-world; Keil and Delitzsch take the reservation of heaven and the gift of earth as a fundamental characteristic of the history after the flood.

debates: What does it mean that the earth is given to the children of men? Keil and Delitzsch make it a characteristic of post-flood history; Wesley makes it an assertion of title, God being Lord and governor of both realms; Clarke dates it from the expulsion from paradise as a grant to till and eat; Spurgeon proposes two senses, one in which God restrains his power because he gave his creatures free agency and permits them their own devices, another in which the clause grounds the promise that his people shall fill the earth.

Who are the dead that do not praise? Clarke confines them to the idolaters just described, dying in their sins; Gill excludes both the dead in sin and departed saints, whose souls praise continually and lack only bodily organs until the resurrection; Spurgeon takes it of this world alone, where no gospel ministry rises from the tomb; Ellicott names the land of silence as the under-world and Wesley as the grave.
outliers: Clarke traces the word that the older English versions use here to a root meaning to cover or conceal, so that it once named merely the hidden obscure place and only later came to express the place of endless torment, and he quotes two old renderings that use it.
Spurgeon observes that the singers of the consecrated choir steal away one by one and their music is missed, so that those who remain have need to sing all the more earnestly.
Clarke closes by asking for further blessings before death so that the living may praise as monuments of mercy, standing in the place of fathers whose tongues are silent in the grave.
themes: heaven reserved and earth handed over
divine power restrained to leave room for human agency
praise described as the work of the living
an old word for the grave rescued by etymology
a psalm ending where it began, on the honour of the name
